column3: The other leg is b=√(c²−4²). Equate the two expressions for triangle area: (1/2)(4)b=(1/2)ch, so h=4b/c.
column4: A nondegenerate right triangle needs c>4. Units stay centimetres because the leg product is divided by the hypotenuse.

column3: Let legs a,b and hypotenuse c. The altitude condition gives ab=12c. Since a+b=p−c, square to obtain (p−c)²=a²+b²+2ab=c²+24c. Cancel c² and solve p²=2c(p+12).
column4: For fixed altitude 12, the smallest hypotenuse is 24 at the isosceles right triangle, whose perimeter is 24+24√2. The geometric perimeter bound excludes algebraically possible but impossible triangles.

column3: Break at x=−5 and x=1/2. The expression abs(2x−1)−abs(x+5) is 6−x for x<−5, −3x−4 for −5≤x<1/2, and x−6 for x≥1/2. Equating each to 3 gives candidates 3,−7/3,9.
column4: Discard 3 from the first interval because it is not below −5; the other two candidates satisfy their intervals and the original equation.

column3: The reverse triangle inequality gives abs(x−1)−abs(x−3)≤abs((x−1)−(x−3))=2.
column4: An expression bounded above by 2 cannot be at least 5. This avoids a longer unnecessary case split.

column2: An even graph with zeros x=±1,±3, height 3 at 0, and local peaks of height 1 at x=±2; range [0,∞).
column3: Put r=abs(x). Then f=abs(r²−4r+3)=abs((r−1)(r−3)). Use r²−4r+3 for 0≤r≤1 or r≥3, and −r²+4r−3 for 1≤r≤3.
column4: Plot on r≥0, reflect across the y-axis, and retain upward tails. The outer absolute value reflects only the negative quadratic section.

column2: g(x)=−3 for abs(x)≤1; 2x²−5 for 1≤abs(x)≤2; 3 for abs(x)≥2.
column3: Let u=x². For u≤1 both u−1 and u−4 are nonpositive; their absolute-value difference is −3. For 1≤u≤4 the difference is (u−1)−(4−u)=2u−5. For u≥4 it is 3.
column4: The graph is even and continuous at x=±1,±2, with range [−3,3]. The outer regions are horizontal, not unbounded parabolas.

column2: The entire closed third quadrant {x≤0,y≤0}, together with the ray y=x≥0.
column3: Use x+abs(x)=2max(x,0). Equality says max(x,0)=max(y,0). If both x,y are nonpositive, both sides vanish. If the common value is positive, x and y must be equal and positive.
column4: Include both negative coordinate-axis rays and the origin. This relation is a region plus a ray, not a single function graph.

column2: For xy≥0, the region is abs(x−y)≤1. For xy≤0, it is abs(x)≤1 and abs(y)≤1; include the boundaries.
column3: With the same signs, abs(x−y)=abs(abs(x)−abs(y)), so the left side becomes 2abs(x−y). With opposite signs it becomes abs(x)+abs(y)+abs(abs(x)−abs(y))=2max(abs(x),abs(y)).
column4: Sketch a diagonal strip in quadrants I and III, joined by the two closed unit squares in quadrants II and IV. The two descriptions agree on the axes.

column2: (a) 1/x for x≤−1, x for −1≤x<0, 1/x for 0<x≤1, x for x≥1; (b) sin x on [π/4+2kπ,5π/4+2kπ], cos x elsewhere; (c) 2+abs(x) for abs(x)≤2, x² for abs(x)≥2.
column3: (a) Solve x=1/x at ±1 and compare the two candidates on each side of zero. (b) sin x−cos x=√2 sin(x−π/4), which determines the upper curve. (c) First max(2+x,2−x)=2+abs(x); compare with x² using r²=r+2 at r=2.
column4: For (a), exclude x=0 and use range [−1,0)∪[1,∞). For (b), the range is [−√2/2,1] and period 2π. For (c), the range is [2,∞). The maximum always chooses the higher candidate, including negative values.

column3: (a) A maximum equals 1 when both entries are at most 1 and at least one equals 1. (b) The upper bound requires x≤1 and 2y≤1; the lower bound requires at least one of x,2y to be at least −1. (c) Apply the equality rule to x and y².
column4: Part (b) is a filled union of horizontal/vertical strips, whereas (a,c) are boundary rays and segments. All inequalities here are non-strict, so retain their edges.

column3: Change each factor to natural logarithms: (ln3/ln2)(ln4/ln3)…(ln32/ln31). Every intermediate logarithm cancels, leaving ln32/ln2=log₂32=5.
column4: Cancellation works because consecutive numerator and denominator logarithms match and none is zero.

column3: Let s=√(x²+1). Since (s−x)(s+x)=1 and s>abs(x), f(−x)=ln(s−x)=−ln(s+x)=−f(x). To invert, e^y=x+√(x²+1) and e^(−y)=√(x²+1)−x; subtract the equations.
column4: Both log arguments are positive for every real x. The inverse is sinh y, so f is the real inverse hyperbolic sine.

column3: ln(x²−2x−2)≤0 means 0<x²−2x−2≤1. The positivity condition gives x<1−√3 or x>1+√3. The upper bound gives (x−1)²≤4, so −1≤x≤3; intersect.
column4: Keep the outer endpoints because log1=0 is allowed, but exclude the inner roots because log0 is undefined.

column3: Suppose log₂5=p/q for positive integers p,q. Then 2^(p/q)=5, so 2^p=5^q. The left side is even and the right side odd, a contradiction.
column4: The positivity p>0 follows from log₂5>0; rationality would allow a positive integer denominator q.

column3: Let the total distance be 2d. Time is d/30+d/60=d/20 hours, so average speed is (2d)/(d/20)=40.
column4: The two speeds act over equal distances, not equal times; their arithmetic mean 45 mi/h is therefore inappropriate.

column3: Choose f(u)=u² and g(x)=h(x)=1. Then [f∘(g+h)](x)=f(2)=4, whereas (f∘g)(x)+(f∘h)(x)=f(1)+f(1)=2.
column4: A single valid counterexample disproves the proposed universal distributive law.

column2: 7ⁿ−1=6(1+7+⋯+7^(n−1)), hence divisible by 6 for every positive integer n.
column3: Expand (7−1)(1+7+⋯+7^(n−1)); adjacent powers cancel, leaving 7ⁿ−1. The parenthesized sum is an integer.
column4: This geometric-series factorization proves the claim without relying on several numerical examples. Inductively, 7^(n+1)−1=7(7ⁿ−1)+6 gives the same result.

column3: For n=1 the identity is 1=1. Assume the sum through 2n−1 is n². Adding the next odd number 2n+1 gives n²+2n+1=(n+1)².
column4: The base case and induction step prove all positive integers; geometrically, each added odd-length border enlarges an n×n square to an (n+1)×(n+1) square.

column3: The initial exponent is 2. Each step applies f0(u)=u² to the current output, doubling the exponent: 2,4,8,16,…. If f_n=x^(2^(n+1)), squaring yields x^(2^(n+2)).
column4: Induction matches the indexing f0=x²; writing x^(2^n) would be off by one.

column3: The formula holds at n=0. If f_n=A/B, then f0(f_n)=1/(2−A/B)=B/(2B−A); substituting A=(n+1)−nx and B=(n+2)−(n+1)x produces the formula for n+1. Each composition retains old excluded inputs and adds the new pole (n+3)/(n+2).
column4: Draw the four rational curves with their true domain exclusions: poles approach x=1 from the right and horizontal asymptotes n/(n+1) approach y=1 from below; earlier excluded poles become holes in later simplified formulas. At x=1 every iterate equals 1; at a fixed admissible x≠1, f_n(x)→1 because f_n−1=(x−1)/((n+2)−(n+1)x).
